Hooghly.— No. 12418L.A.— 2nd July 1958.— 
Whereas it appears to the Governor that land 
is likely to be needed for a public purpose, not being 
a purpose of the Union, namely, for excavation of 
Minor River Gangur from chainage 112*60 to 
chainage 145*00 in connection with the Damodar 
Flood Control Project in the village of Inchura, 
jurisdiction list No. 14, thana Pandua, district 
Hooghly, it is hereby notified that a piece of land 
comprising part of cadastral survey plot Nos. 25, 
85, 86, 88, 91 to 96, 100, 132, 133, 205 to 207, 

209, 210, 217 to 222, 226, 227, 246 to 254, 266, 

267, 278, 372, 550, 551, 571, 574, 577 to 579, 

581 and 2115, and measuring, more or less, 4*47 

acres, is likely to be needed for the aforesaid public 
purpose ,at the expense of the Damodar Valley 
Corporation, within the aforesaid village of Inchura. 

This notification is made, under the provisions of 
section 4 of Act I of 1894, to all whom it may 
concern. 

A plan of the land may be inspected in the office 
of the Special Land Acquisition Collector, Damodar 
Valley Project, Chinsura (Hooghly). 

In exercise of the powers conferred by the 
aforesaid section the Governor is pleased to autho- 
rise the officers for the time being engaged in the 
undertaking, with their servants and workmen, to 
ter upon and survey the land and do all other acts 
|un*ed or permitted by that section. 

In exercise of the powers conferred by section 
(4) of the Land Acquisition Act I of 1894, as 
lended by Act XXXVIII of 1923, the Govei;nor 
pleased to direct that the provisions ,,bf section 5A 
the Act shall not a{>ply to this case. 

By order of the Governor, 

S. C. CHATTERJEE,

8TATEMEHT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 

Under the Bihar and West Bengal (Transfeired I'erritories) Act, 1950, 
certain territories from the State of Bihar were transferred to West Bengal. 
But in view of the provisions of section 48, read with seed ion 2(c) of the 
said Act, almost all the Bihar laws including enactments, regulations, 
ordinances, notifications, etc., which were applicable to the transferred terri- 
tories ]»efore the dale of iransfer continue to lie in force theie. A few West 
Bengal laws only were extended there on grounds of expediency. Tt has, 
howt'viM , given rise to some lamfusion and is causing administrative 
sciiflicult ies. 

The ol)ject of tlie Bill is to bring the transferred territories umler the 
same set of laws which are applicable to the rest of W^est Bengal as far 
as possible and thus to remove the difficulties. It is, therefore, proi)osed to 
repeal the Bihar laws in force there and to extend West Bengal laws. In 
view of tile s])erial circumstances, it is proposed to retain certain Bihar laws 
for some time m(>re and to extend some \Vest Bengal laws at a later date. 

The Bill hasS been drafted accordingly.

(2) If any person refuses to comply with an order under

(J) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law 
for the time being in force, no person shall be entitled to claim

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 

The Damodar Valley Corporation Act, 1948 (XIV of 1948) provides for 
the levy of rates by the Corporation for bulk supply of water to the Government. 
It also contemplates retail supply of water to cultivators and other consumers by 
the Government at rates which shall be fixed by the Government after consultation 
with the Corporation, 

It is thus open to cultivators to take or not to take the water that is available 
for irrigation purposes. As it is necessary to ensure the fullest utilisation of 
water available for irrigation purposes, the present Bill has been drawn up to 
make provision for compulsory levy of water rates on the owners or occupiers 
of lands within the limits of the Damodar Valley or within the area of the 
operation of the Corporation, for making available to such owners or occupiers 
water for irrigating their lands during the kharif season or the rabi season by the 
construction and maintenance of canals and distributaries, and for certain other 
matters ancillary thereto and connected therewith.

THE WEST BENGAL PROHIBITION OF THE EVICTION OF THE 
WORKERS’ FAMILY (TEA ESTATES) BILL, 1958. 

A 

BILL 

to iiroliibit the eviction of a worker s family or members thereof from a tea 
estate on the di^mtssal of the head of the family. 

Whereas it is expedient to prohibit the eviction of ii worker'^ fiiiiiil.v 
or members thereof from ii tea estate on the j>roiind that tlie head the 
family has been dismissed from service ; 

It is hereby enacted in the Ninth Year of the Republic of India hv flic 
Leg-islature of West Bengal, as follows: — 

1. (i) This Act may be called the West Bengal rrohibilion «d tlic 
Eviction of the AVorkers' Family (Tea Estates) Act, 11F)8. 

(2) It shall apply to all tea estates situated in West Ben cal and as 
defined under this Act, 

(J) It shall come into force immediately. 

2. Definition . — In this Act unless the context otherwise rei)uiif ' — 

(a) ‘Tea Estate’’ means any land used or intended to be used for 
growing tea, which measures twenty-five aires or Biure uinl 
whereon thirty or more persons are employed or were emploNcd 
on any day of the preceding twelve months, 

(h) ‘‘Employer” means the person who has the ultimate (ontrol ov«r 
the affairs of the tea estate and where the affairs of am tea 
estate are entrusted to any other person (whether (.died a 
managing agent, manager, superintendent or hv am oWws 
name), such other person shall be deemed to be the ciuidoyei m 
relation to the tea estate

((•) “Worker” means a person employed in a tea estate for hire or

3 . l*rt>hibiiit>n e/ rrtrffon, — So long as any member of a worker’s

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 

The j)ractice followed by fhe employers in the tea gardens of evicting 
the entire worker's family on the dismissal of the head of the family and 
claimed by them as a mutter of right accruing from usage was declared 
to be illegal and ultra arcs by the Labour Ap])ellate Tribunal some years 
ago. Since tlien the Government of India as well as tlie State Government 
have declared the said jiractice lo be illegtil and tlie State Government has 
intimated its o]»inion to the employers. In s])ite of that even now the 
said jiractiee is being folloM'ed by the employers in (‘ertain cases, lleiu’c 
it is necessary to enact a law expressly prohibiting the said practice and 
providing for penalties in cases of contravention of the jirovisions of the 
law. The Bill has been drafted with the above obje(‘t in view.

It is estimated that aljout 40,000 milch animals are kept in Calcuttii an,l

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 

Under section 3 of the Chandernagorc (Assimilation of Laws) Act, 1955 
all State laws which extend to or are in force in West Bengal generally would 
extend to Chandernagorc. According to a recent decision of the Calcutta High 
Court the word "generally" admits of no exception and consequently only those 
State laws which were in force in the whole of West Bengal would extend to 
Chandernagorc. 

The West Bengal Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 does not apply to 
the municipal areas of Calcutta and Howrah. The West Bengal L^d 
Development and Planning Act, 1948 and the West Bengal Estates Acquisition 
Act 1953 do not apply to the municipal area of Calcutta. These Acts oo 
not ’apply to the whole of West Bengal and do not therefOTC extend to 
Chandwnagore. As it is necessary to extend these Acts to Chandernagorc 
suitable provisions have to be made by amending the Chandernagorc 
(Assimilation of Laws) Act, 1955. 

The Bill has been drawn up accordingly.

for regulating exhibitions in West Bengal by means of cinematograph, other 
than public exhibitions, published at pages 1973-1976 of Part I of the Calcuitu 
Gazette, Extraordinurv. dated the 1 0th August 1956, namely:—

ORDER 

No. 5920P.- 19th July 1958. — In exercise of the power codfierred 
by sub-section (2) of section 3 of the West Bengal Cinemas (Rcjgulation) Act, 
1954 (West Bengal Act XXXIX of 1954), read with section 9 of the said Act, 
the Governor having considered it necessary so to do, is pleased to make this 
order for regulating private exhibitions in West Bengal by means of cinematograph, 
namely; — 


Order 

1 . ( / ) This Order may be called the West Bengal Cinematograph (Regu- 
lation of Private Exhibition) Order, 1958. 

(2) It shall come into force at once. 

2. In this Order unless the context otherwise requires, — 

(i/) “the Act” means the West Bengal Cinemas (Regulation) Act, 1954; 

(h) “private cinematograph exhibition” means an indoor or open air 

exhibition by means of cinematograph, admission to which is res- 
tricted by issue of invitations, tokens or cards, or is restricted to 
members of a particular club, institution or organisation; 

(r) “section” means a section of the Act. 

3. Private cinematograph exhibition shall be regulated in accordance with 
the following rules and conditions, namely: 

Rules and Conditions 

1. Appliraiioti for license. — Any person desirous of holding a private 
cinematograph exhibition expected to jlic attended by more than twenty-five 
persons at a time shall submit a written application to the District Magistrate 
at least seven days in advance for the grant of a license. The application shall 
contain the following particulars: — 

(i) name and address of the applicant; 

(/7) name, if any, of (he film or general description thereof; 

(Hi) the hour fixed for each show and its duration; 

(iv) the venue of the exhibition; 



Pabt I] 


THE CAL. GAZ., EXTRY., JULY 19, 1968 


(v) whether the venue provides for the safety precautions referr 
, condition 4 of the Schedule attached to the form of Hcl., 
private cinematograph exhibition; • 

(v/) the period for which the license is required; 

(v//) the purpose of the exhibition; 

(vh7) the maximum number of invitees proposed to be admitted in each'^ 

(ijr) declaration that the film is certified for unrestricted exhibition o 
adults only or exempted from censorship by the Central Governn 

(jr) name of the producer of the film; 

(xi) the country in which the film has been produced. 

2. Grant of license. — (7) On receipt of an application for a priva 
cinematograph exhibition the District Magistrate may at his discretion grant t= 
the applicant a license for such private cinematograph exhibition as early a: 
possible in the form appended to these rules and subject to the conditions sci 
forth in the Schedule attached thereto for such period as may be considered by 
him to be necessary for holding the exhibition. 

(2) No fee shall be charged for granting such license. 

(.?) When a license granted under sub-rule (/) is either lost or accidentally 
destroyed, a duplicate of the original license may be granted on receipt of a 
written application free of any charge. 

3. No license required for private cinematoftraph exhibition where the 
number of people attending does not exceed twenty-five . — No license shall be 
required for holding any private cinematograph exhibition where the number of 
people attending the exhibition at any one time docs not exceed twenty-five.

Conditions to he attached to a license for private cinematograph exhibition 

1. This license shall remain in force only for 

2. No lilni which has not been eertilied by the Central Board of Film 
Censors as suitable for public exhibition or has not been exempted from the 
provisions of section of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 (XXXVll of 1952), 
shall be exhibited or permitted to be exhibited. 

3. No film, which has not been certified by the Central Board of Film 
Censors as suitable for public exhibition restricted to adults only, shall be 
exhibited or permitted to be exhibited to a person who is not an adult as defined 
in clause (a) of section 2 of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 (XXXVII of 1952). 

- 4. The following safety precautions shall be observed in case of 35 mm. 
cinematograph film; 

(a) only non-inflammable films shall be exhibited or permitted to be 
exhibited; 

(/)) no drapery and no combustible material, other than such material as 
may compose the floor, shall be within six leet of the cinematograph; 

(f) a bucket of sand and two buckets of water shall be placed close to 
the cinematograph and a large sponge shall be kept in one of the 
buckets of water; 

(d) not more than two hundred pounds of film shall be kept in any place 
where such exhibition is being made, and all such films shall be kept 
in securely closed fire-resisting receptacles; 

(r*) no exhibition shall be held in a tent or in any shelter or structure 
composed of, or covered with, combustible material or of a move- 
able character unless the cinematograph is operated from outside 
and at a distance of at least six feet from such shelter or structure. 

5. A licensee niay shift the venue of the exhibition from place to place 
after giving due intimation of his programme and itineniry in advance to the 
Hcensing authority provided that all the rules and safety precautions are duly 
observOT.

24-P;irganas. 

In exercise of the powers conferred by the said 
section, read with the said notification, the Governor 
is pleased to authorise the officers for the time 
being engaged in the undertaking, with their servants 
and workmen, lo enter upon and survey the land 
and do all other acts required or permitted by that 
section. 

Arly person interested in so much of the above 
land, as is not waste and arable, who has any 
objection to the acquisition thereof, may, within 
thirty days after the date on which public notice 
of the siibisianee of this notification is given in the 
locality, file an objection, in writing, before the 
Collector of 24-Parganas (Land Acquisition Depart- 
ment, Alipore). 

In exercise of the powers conferred by section 
17(4) of the Land Acquisition Act, I of 1894, as 
amended by Act XXXVIII of 1923, read with the 
aforesaid notification, the Governor is pleased to 
direct that the provisions of section 5A of the Act 
shall not apply to the waste and arable portions of 
the land in this case. 

By order of the Governor, 

S. C. CHATTERJEE, 

Special Officer and Dy, Secy, to the 
Govt, of West Bengal (ex-officio).

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 

The Ccmrt-feeti Act, 1870, ccmtaiiis on provisions barring* the Courts m 
West Bengral from accepting a document even if it is stamped with Conn- 
fees purchased outside the State. This may result in loss of revenue to tins 
State* It is necessary to amend the Court-fees Act, 1871), suitably to pre- 
vent this loss to the State. Afjrain, there is no provision in the said A(‘t 
authorising* the High Court, while dealing with an application for leave in 
appeal to the Supreme (’oiiH under Article 133 of the i'onstitutmn, 

to make an order for the recovery of deficit Court-fees in any case wheiv 
the High Court finds that the subject-matter of the suit or appeal \Niis 
undervalued in the lower Courts, and consequently, an insufficient ainouiii 
of Court-fees was paid. This also causes loss of revenue to the State. It 
is ncHiessarv to amend the Act authorising the High Court to ordiT the 
payment of deficit Court-fees in suitable cases. 

Neither the Special Marriage Act, 1954, nor the Hindu Marriage Act. 
1955, has any provision prescribing the fee payable on a petition for restitu- 
tion of conjugal rights, judicial se]»araiion, or divorce, or on u rieinoran.lnm 
of appeal filed under either of the Acts. It is desirable that a fixed fee 
should be prescribed by amending Schedule II of the Court-fees Act, ISTti. 

The Bill has been drawn up for the purposes indicated above.

makes the following Order, namely: — 

1. Short title, extent and commencement. — (/) This Order may be callec 
the Cement Control Order, 1958. 

C?) It extends to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir 

(J) It shall come into force on the first day of July 1958. 

2. Definitions. — In this Order, unless the context otherwise requires, — 

(«) “cement” means any variety of cement manufactured in India, and 
includes rapid hardening cement and low heat cement, but does not 
include waterprenrf cenjcnt and white and coloured cement (othei 
than grey Portland cement) or any other variety of cement which the 
Central Govemnjcnt may, by notification in the Official Gazette, 
specify as not being cement for the purpose of this Order; 

(/)) “Corporation” means the State Trading Coqioration of India (Private) 
Limited; 

(c) “producer” means any person who manufactures cement. 

3. Proilucers to sell cement to Corporation. — (I) Every producer shall 
sell — 


(a) the entire quantity of cement held in stock by him on the date of 
commencement of this Order; and 

(h) the entire quantity of cement which may be produced by Mm during 
a period of three years from the date of commencement of this 
Order; cxeept such quantity ;is may be mutually agreed upon from 
time to time between him and the Central Government; 

to the rorpt)ration, and deliver the same to such person or persons as may 
be specified by the ( orporation in this behalf from time to time. 

(2) Notwithstanding any contraet to the contrary, no producer shall dispose 
of cement held in stock oi prmluccd by him cxeept in accordance with the 
provisions of sub-clause (/). 

4. Cement not to he removed from premises of producer withimt permission. 
— (/) No producer shall remove or permit the removal of any cement, whether 
sold or unsold, from any part of his premises to any place outside his premises 
except with the written permission of the Central Government or such officer as 
may be specified by it in this behalf. 

(2) Nothing contained in sub-clause (/) shall apply in respect of any cement 
sold to the Corporation in pursuance of clause 3. 

5. Maintenance and production of hooks of accounts, etc., by producers.— 

( 7 ) Every prixluccr shall keep such books, accounts and records relating to the 
production of cement as the Central Government may require.

NOTIFICATION 

No, 6256P. — 31st July 1958. — Whereas for the 
prevention of disturbances of the public tranquillity 
and of riots and affrays within the area described 
tn the Schedule below, hereinafter referred to as the 
said area, the Subdivisional Magistrate, Alipurduar, 
issued an order, dated the 3rd June 1958, under 
section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 
1898 (Act V of 1898), restraining one Shri Nani 
Gopal Bhattacharyya and the members of the 
general public from holding hats in the said area; 

And whereas it appears to the State Govemmtmt 
iQat there is still a likelihood of riots and affrays 
Within the said area and that it is necessary to further 
continue in force the said order of the Subdivisional 
Magistrate, Alipurduar; 

Now, therefore, in exercise of the power conferred 
SBb-section (6) of section 144 of the Code of Cli- 
dal ProQpdure^ 1898 (Act V of 1898), the G-'

is pleased to direct that the said order of the Sub- 
divisional Magistrate, Alipurduar, dated the 3rd June 
1958, under the said section, shall remain in force, 
until the 2nd October 1958.

NOTIFICATION 

No. 4777W.T.^ — 4th August 1958. — In exercise of the 
powers conferred by the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 (IV 
of 1939), aild, ill particular, by sections 21, 21J, 41 
and 68 thereof, the Governor is pleased to make the 
following amendments in the Bengal Motor Vehicles 
Rules, 1940, published with notification No. 1930P1., 
dated the 21st September 1940, at pages 2655-2829 of 
Part I of the Calcutta Gazette, dated the 10th October 
1940, as subsequently amended, namely: — 

Amendments 

1. After clause (/) of rule 2 of the said rules, 
insert the following new clause, namely: — 

“(//) ‘Director, Public Vehicles Department, 
Calcutta’, includes any other officer or officers 
of the said department, if specially authorised 
by the Director.”, and 

2. In the said rules and in the Schedules annexed to 
the said rules, for the words “Deputy Commissioner of 
Police, Public Vehicles Department, Calcutta” wherever 
they occur, substitute the words “Director, Public 
Vehicles Department, Calcutta”. 

By order of the Governor, 

G. C. MALLIK, 

Asst, Secy, to the Govt, of West Bengal.

Transport 
NOTIFICATION 

No. 4902W.T. — 7th August 1958. — In exercise of the power conferred by 
sub-section (7) and, in particular, by clause {za) of sub-section (2) of section 
68 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 (IV of 1939), the Governor is pleased 
to make the following amendments in the Bengal Motor Vehicles Rules, 1940, 
published with notification No. 1930P1., dated the 21st September 1940, at 
pages 2655-2829 of Part I of the Calcutta Gazette of the 10th October 1940, 
as subsequently amended, after previous publication as required by sub-section 
(/) of section 133 of the said Act, namely: — 

Amendments 

In the said rules — 

(1) after rule 55, insert the following new rulei namely:— 

“55A. Route or area for stage Carriage permits — publication thereof.— 

The Regional Transport Authority or the State Transport Autho- 
rity, if it decides to grant permits for stage carriage on any route 
or area, shall publish in a newspaper or newspapers of standing 
in the region, particulars of such route or area, the number of 
permits to be granted and the date appointed for receipt of 
applications for such permits”; and

(2) for sub-rule (h) of rule 57, substitute the following, namely: — 

"(/>) It shall be sufficient compliance with the provisions of sub-section 
of section 57 of the Act, if the substance of or the particulars 
of applications for permits for stage carriages or public carriers 
or for their renewal are posted on the official notice board of the 
t)irice of the Regional Transport Authority or the State Transport 
Authority not less than thirty days before the date appointed for 
the receipt of representations: 

Provided that in the case of application for permits for stage carriages, 
a notice shall further be published in a newspaper or newspapers 
of standing in the region, specifying the total number of appli- 
cations received for such route or area, the place where their 
particulars may be available for inspection, the date appointed 
for receipt of representations and the date, time and place, on 
which and at which applications and representations received will 
be considered.”

(a) to declare the said area to be a protected area; 

(h) to specify the tenth day of August 1958 as the day on and after which 
no person who was not immediately before the said day resident in 
the said area shall be therein except in accordance with the terms of 
a permit referred to in sub-section (2) of the said section; and 

(c) to specify each of (/) the Station Director, All India Radio, Calcutta,

Appeal from Original Decree No. 235 of 1957 (Election Appeal) 

Appeal against the decree of Shri S. M. Banerjee, District Judge, of zil 
Midnapore. as the Election Tribunal confstituted under the Representat 
of the People Act, 1951, in Election Petition Case No. 447 of 1957, da

SUDHANSU SfiKHAR Panda — Petitioner Appellant, 

versus 

Natendra Nath Das and Another — Respondents. 

For Appellant: Mr. D. N. Das and

For Respondents: Mr. S. K. Das and 

Mr. B. K. Panda for respondent No. 1. 

Mr. N. C. Chakra vartty for respondent No. 2. 


H appellant before us was the unsuccessful cand 

rvJn r! Election from the Contai North Legislative Asscnibl 

Sd West Bengal. The election was held on March 7, 1951 

havin!l ^ Jto. 1, who was the rival candidate, was declared elected, hi 

against the appellant’s 20,523. Respondcn 

tNo. 2 was the Returning Officer. 


In or about the beginning of May 1957 the appellant applied for settinf 
aside the election of respondent No. 1 and for a further declaration that hj 
(the appellant) had been duly elected. The application was duly sent bf 
registered pewt to the Election Commission, New Delhi, which received it f 
May 3, 1957 It was registered as Election Petition No. 447 of 1957. 
an order, dated July 2, 1957, the Chief Election Commissioner fixed the tot** J 
the petition at Midnapore before Shri Surendra Mohan Banerjee (Shri S. W- 
Banerjee), District Judge, Midnapore, who was constituted the one-man Tribuna 
or the purpose. The 20th July 1957 was fixed as the date for the first 
ance of the parties before the Tribunal and appropriate notices were issued 



kKT lA] 


'J'HE CAL. GAZ., EXTRY., AUGUST 22. 1968 


2836 


;m accordingly. The petition was forwarded to the Tribunal on July 10, 
57, and there the parties appeared and the respondents duly filed their written 
itements. 

The petition has been dismissed by the Tribunal on the preliminary ground 
non-compliance with the provisions of section 117 of the Representation 
the People Act, 1951 (Central Act No. XLIII of 1951). 'Fhc propriety 
this decision is questioned in this appeal. 

The matter arose upon Order No. 2 of the Chiel Election Commissioner, 
led May 14, 1957, wherein he observed, inter alia, as follows: 

“The Treasury Chalan, enclosed with the petition, is defective inasmuch 
as it does not specifically mention that the amount has been deposited 
in favour of the Secretary, Flection Commission. This may make it 
difficult for the costs, if any, ordered against the petitioner to be 
realised out of the deposits.” 

d also upon the specific objection, taken by respondent No. 2 in his written 
tement, to the effect that “as no requisite deposit has been made in favour 
the Secretary to the Election Commission, provision of section 117 has not 
en complied with and as such the petition is liable to be dismissed.” 

The relevant facts lie within a very narrow compass and they stand as stated 
reunder: 

The election petition, as we have said abttve, was filed about the beginning 
of May 1957, its verification being dated April 30, 1957. On that 
date, it appears the petitioner deposited with the Reserve Bank of 
India, Calcutta, sum of Rs. 1,000 by a duly receipted chalan of that 
dale which may be set out hereunder as follows: 



2 h ;{0 


THE CAL. GAZ., EXTHY., AllGU«T 22, Ims 


ll’AKT 




t*AET XA] 


TilE CAL. OAZ.. EXTRY., AUGUST 22, 1968 


2837 




2S:J8 


THE CAL. 0A7.., EXTBY., AUGUST 22. 1968 


[Part lA 


The receipted chalan or the Government Treasury receipt, as it is designated 
by the statute (vide section 117), undoubtedly shows deposits of Rs. 1,000 by 
the petitioner in connection with “an election petition for setting aside the 
election result of the Contai North Constituency, district Midnapore, in the 
Legislative Assembly Constituency in the State of West Bengal.” The money 
also appears to have been credited under the Head of Account relating, inter alia, 
to “Deposits for Llcction Petitions.” The point is whether section 1 1 7 of the 
Representation of the People Act, 1951, has been complied with, so as to 
sustain the appellant’s election petition. 

Section 117 is in the following terms: 

“Deposits of security — The j^titioner shall enclose with the petition a Gov- 
ernment Treasury receipt showing that 'a deposit of one thousand 
rupees has been made by him either in a Government Treasury or in 
the Reserve Bank of India in favour of the Secretary to the Election 
Commission as security for the costs of the petition.” 

It thus requires the petitioner to enclose with his petition “a Government Treasury 
receipt showing that a deposit of one thousand rupees has been made by him 
either in a Government Treasury or in the Reserve Bank of India in favour 
of the Secretary to the Election Commission as security for the costs of the 
petition.” 

Analysing the requirements under the section, it is clear that the Government 
Treasury receipt, or the Treasury receipt, as it is usually called, which is to 
accompany the election petition, must show a deposit by the petitioner of one 
thousand rupees — 

(/) in a Government Treasury or in the Reserve Bank of India, 

(/■/) in favour of the Secretary to the Election Commission, and 

(///) as security for the costs of the petition. 

Admittedly, in this case. Treasury receipt was enclosed with the petition. 
That receipt also shows deposit of one thousand rupees by the petitioner in the 
Reserve Bank of India. It does not, however, show that the deposit was made 
in favour of the Secretary to the Election Commission or as security for the costs 
of the petition. The question is, whether this defect (which is prima facie 
there) is fatal to the maintainability of the petition. 

The Tribunal has answered the question in the affirmative and the point is 
whether its view is right. 

The answer depends on section 90(3) of the Representation of the People 
Act, 1951, read with section 117. This latter section has been fully set out 
above. We need not discuss it at this stage. The other section, however, 
namely, section 90(3) which is in these terms, — 

“The Tribunal shall dismiss an election which does not comply with the 
provisions of section 81, section 82 or section 117 notwithstanding 
that it has not been dismissed by the Election Commission under 
section 85.” 

is plainly mandatory, particularly when it is remembered that, by the amendment 
of 1956 [vide section 51(d) of Central Act 27 of 19561 the word “shall” 
introduced in the section in place of the word “may” which occurred in the 


Part IA] 


THE CAL. GAZ., EXTRY., AUGUST 22, 1968 


28H9 


corresponding provision section 90(4) before (he said amendment and it leaves 
no discretion to the Tribunal and, in case of non-compliance with, inter alia, 
section 117, the Tribunal is bound to dismiss the petition. It is, therefore, 
necessary to enquire whether there has been in the present case non-compliance 
with section 117 and such non-compliance as comes within the meaning and 
mischief of section 90(3). 

We have pointed out above that the Government Treasury receipt, enclosed 
by the petitioner with his election petition to comply with section 1 1 7 of the 
Act, is prima facie detective in that it does not show deposit of the amount 
(one thousand rupees) in favour of the Secretary to the Election Commission 
or as sescurity for the costs of the petition. That position cannot be controverted. 


It is argued, however, on behalf of the petitioner (appellant) that the defect, 
as disclosed above, is merely one of form and not of substance and that, as such, 
it should be disregarded for purposes of section 90(3). The basis of this argu- 
ment is that section 117, so far, at least, as the form or manner of deposit is 
concerned, is not mandatory but merely directory and substantial compliance 
with it in that respect ought to be sufficient (vide Punjab Co-operation Bank 
Limited, Amritsar versus Income Tax Commission, Lahore L.R. 67 LA. 464 at 
page 476) and no strict compliance ought to be demanded and, in that view, 
the Treasury receipt in the present case should be regarded as of requisite 
compliance with section 117 for purposes of section 90(3). 


In the view, which we arc taking, it is unnecessary to express any opinion 
on the petitioner’s above basic argument on the point and to decide whether 
the relevant part of section 117 is mandatory or directory as, in our opinion, 
there has been, in this case, not even substantial compliance with the statute 
(section 117), there being nothing in the receipt or in the materials, placed 
before us, from which it can be necessarily or even reasonably construed that the 
deposit is in favour of the Secretary to the Election Commission or as security 
for the costs of the petition. In the absence of any material, showing that the 
deposit money would be available to the Secretary to the Election Commission 
as or by way of security for costs of the petition, it would not be proper tt) hold 
that the statute has even been substantially complied with. Nothing, indeed, 
could be placed before us to enable us to hold or to warrant a finding that, 
under the above deposit, as it stands, the money would be payable to the 
Secretary to the Election Commission or that the Reserve Bank would pay it 
to him or that the said officer, even if he be paid the money, would hold it or 
would be bound to hold it as security for the costs of the petition. At least, 
the position is one of uncertainty which makes it difficult for the Court to find 
substantial compliance with the statute. Even the theory of substantial com- 
pliance would not, therefore, help the appellant in the present case and so his 
appeal cannot succeed. 


In the above view, we do not deem it necessary to examine the implications 
of the observations of the Supreme Court in Jagannath versus Jaswant Singh 
and Others, A.I.R. 1954 S.C.210 at pages 212 and 214 or to discuss the 
decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada in (1891) 20 Canada Supreme Court 
Reports 26 [Queen’s County and Prince County (P ^ ) oul 

the English House of Lords in Katherine Yale verw^v The King ( 1 72 1 ) L.R.91U 
or the very recent decision of Sinha, J. in Civil Revision Case No. 2294 of 19. 7 
fBiren Roy versus Bijoyesh Mukherjee and Others) which all appear to be 
dearly distinguishable. 


2S40 


(Part TA 


THE f:AL. (MZ., EXTRV.. AIKJTJST 22, 

In the result, we dismiss this appeal with costs, hearing fee being assessed 
at three gold mohurs for each set of appearing respondents. 

Let a copy of this judgment be forwatded to the Election Commission as 
early as possible.

No. 16858L.Rcf. — 23rd August 1958.— The 
following draft of an amendment which, in exercise 
of the power conferred by section 60 of the West 
Bengal Land Reforms Act, 1955 (West Bengal Act 
X of 1956), the Governor proposes to make in the 
West Bengal Land Reforms (Bargadars) Rules, 1956, 
published with notification No. 9796L.Ref., dated the 
Isl June 1956, as subsequently amended (hereinafter 
referred to as the said rules), is hereby published, as 
required by sub-section (1) of the said section, for 
the information of persons likely to be affected 
thereby. 

Notice is hereby given that the draft will be taken 
into consideration on or after the 4th September 1958 
and any objection or suggestion with respect thereto 
which may be received by the undersigned before 
that date shall be considered.

rules, substitute the wor4s “^ttlement Officer having 
jurisdiction over the area in which the land is 
situated” for the words “Director of Land Records 
and Sumeys.”

Court, Government Treasury, etc. 

GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 
LABOUR DEPARTMENT 
ORDER 

No. 3632-l.R. ilRI9L-23 158. — 28lh Augu.st J958. — Whereas an industrial 
dispute exists between the Gayaganga lea E.siaie, P.O. Kamalabagan (Darjeeling), 
hereinafter relerred to as the employer, and its workmen represented by Terai 
t’ha-Bagan Shramik Union, Bhojnarayan Tea Estate, P.O. Kamaia, Darjeeling, 
heremaltcr referred to as the workmen, relating to the matters specified m the 
Second Schedule to the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947); 

And whereas the employei arul the workmen have, under sub-section ( 1 ) ,of 
section KJA of the said Aei, relerred the said dispute to arbitration by an Arbi- 
tration Agreement and have submitted to the State Government under sub-section 
(3) of the said section a copy of the said arbitration agreement: 

Now, therefore, in pursuance ol sub-section f3l of section lOA of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby 
to publish the said arbitration agreement as shown in the Annexure hereto. 


ANNEXURE 

Memorandum of Settlement 

1. Names of parties. — Messrs. Gayaganga 'lea Estate versus Their workmen 
represented by Terai Cha-Bagan Shramik Union. 

2. Representing employers. — Shri Thirani (Management). 


/in»e .•II 


THE CAL. GAZ., EXTRY., AUGUST 29, 


3. Representing employees . — Shu B^ma and Shri H. B. Chettri (Union 
workmen). 

Hon’ble Labour Minister and Deputy Labour Minister, Government of West 
Bengal, were also present. 

4. Short recital of the case. — A dispute between the Management of the 
Gayaganga Tea Estate and its workmen cropped up some time in February 
IQ'SS over the question of task for ridging m section No. 6 of the estate. The 
Management had fixed a task of 20 laggies (Hazri) for the male workmen and 
the workmen failed or refused to do the allotted task and made a representation 
to the Management that the task should be reduced. Parties failed to make any 
settlement in spite of conciliaticm. The Management complained later on that 
certain workmen engaged on other tasks in other sections of the estate had left 
their allotted tasks and joined workmen in section No. 6 or in other sections 
and performed allegedly certain tasks which were not their allotted tasks and 
they refused to pay such workmen wages, etc., for such unauthorised work. 

The Management dismissed seven workmen for disobedience of lawful orders 
and other offences. 

The estate was locked out on 17th March 1958. 


5. Terms of Settlement . — The task for ridging in section No. 6 shall be 
17 laggies (Hazri) per day for male workmen and the Management shall pay 
such workmen who were asked to work in section 6 and who worked there their 
wages and dearness allowance retrospectively on the basis of the above task. 

Four of the seven dismissed workmen shall be reinstated (names will be 
announced by the Management). Three other dismissed workmen (names will 
be given by the Management) shall be allotted some jobs in another establishment 
subject to the conditions that the justifiability or otherwise of their dismissals 
and as to whether they are entitled to reinstatement shall be referred to a person 
of judicial experience along with the following matters for arbitration: 

(/) whether the workmen should be paid any compensation for the period 
of lock-out; 

(ii) whether or not any workmen lelt their tasks and performed other tasks 
in violation of Management's instructions and if the issue is answered 
in the affirmative whether such workmen are entitled to receive 
wages and dearness allowance for such unauthorised work. 

The Arbitrator will be appointed by the Government. The date on which 
the lock-out will be lifted will be notified by the Management, but it will he 
lifted by 21st April 1958. 

Signature of the parties: Thirani (for Management). 

H. B. Chettri (for Union workmen). 

Signature of Conciliation Officer: K. C. Das Gupta. 


Darjeeling; 

The 16th April 1958,

We now take up the respondent No. I’s cross-objection. That is directed 
against the refusal of resjiondeut No. 1 ’s (i)etitioner’8) prayer for declarinu’ 
him duly elected upon the setting aside of the appellant’s election. This 
claim is sought to be supported on the ground that the votes, cast in favour 
of the apiiellant, who has lK*en found to be dis(|ualified under Article 173(b) 
of the Constitution, are “thrown away” or invalid votes and should be left 
out of account in calculating the valid votes under section 101(a) of the 
Jlcpresentation of the People Act, 1951, and as, of the valid votes, so cal- 
culated, the respondent No. 1 has admittedly secured the majority, he should 
be declared elected under the said section, namely, section 101 (a) of the, 
llepreseutation of the People Act, 1951. 

The above argument was very cleverly l>ut by Mr. G. P. Kar, Counsel 
for respondent No. 1, on the apparent authority of a certain English decision 
and certain passages in Halsbury’s Iauch of Enyland, 3rd Edition, to which 
we shall presently refer, but a closer examination betrayed its inherent 
weakness. 

The doctrine of “thrown away’’ votes is based on the principle of a fair 
inference of wilful perverseness on the jiart of the electors, voting for the 
disqualified candidate. That inference, however, is permissible only under 
certain circumstances, namely, where the voters, “before the voting, have 
had or must be deemed to have had noti<-e of the facts, creating the 
<‘iiudidate’s disqualification’’, or, in other words, actual or constructive 
notice of the same, which may arise from the notoriety of the particular 
fact or facts or otherwise. Votes, given without such notiije, would be good 
votes. Neither the case cited by Mr. Kar, namely, Boresford-Ho}»e versv.i 
Lady Sandhurst (1889) 23 Q. B. T).79 nor the passages, idted by him from 
Halsbury’s Loiv.'i of Englnmd , namely, the first part of section 549, page 305, 
Vol. 14, 3rd Fidition, would support any other conclusion. 

Mr. Kai made his submissions under three heads: 

He first contended that “status incapacity’’ or “status disqualification’’ 
as in the case of aliens, infants, etc., stands difiereully from other incapaci- 
ties or disqualifications and should, by itself, be sufficient to lead to the 
intereuc.e of wilful perverseness on the part of (he voters, voting for such 
disqualified candidate. He argued that, in smdi cases, the. dis»]ualificatiou 
is “founded on a positive and definite fact, existing and established at th«‘ 
time «)f the poll so as to lead b) the fair inference of wilful perverseness «)n 
the part of the voters, voting for the dis(|ualified candidate” and, iu 
support of his argument, he relied on the several passages, occurring in the 
earlier part of section 549 of Halsburv’s Laws of Enplnnd, 3rd Edition, 
Vol. 14, where reference is given to footnotes (1). (m) and ‘(n), and also on 
the observations of T^ord Colendge. C.J., in Beiesford-Hope versus Tiodv 
Sandhurst (1889) 23 Q.B.P. 79, at page 94, lines 1 to 10. of the Report . 
Tie submitted that, in such cases, no (piestion of noti(-e would arise and the 
“status dis(|ualification’’ would, bv itself, be sufficient to invalidate the 
votes, cast in favour of the dis(|ualified candidate. 

We are unable to at'cept Mr. Kar’s argument and the authorities citeil 
hy him, do not, in our opinion, supf)ort his extreme contention. The law 
on the point may now be taken t(» be fairly well-settled. The question of 


3008

[Fmw IA 


“thrown away” votes would not und eannot arise unless the votes were cast 
in favour of the disqualified candidate with notice or knowledge of the dis- 
(|ualificutiou or of the facts c-reating the same. Such uotic^e or knowledge 
may be actual or constructive and may arise from the notoriety ui the fact 
on which the disqualifi(;atiuu is bused, or otherwise. But, where the votes 
are cast without notice or knowledge of the basic fact of the particular 
disquulihcution, tlicy would be good voles und would not be thrown awav. 
I’ossibly, notice of the law would not be necessary as every voter may tie 
presumed to know the law, vide Gosling reruns Veley (1847) 7 Q.B.406, at 
page 439 and Lady Sandhurst’s case (1889), 23 (LB.]).79 at page 85. See 
jilso llalsburv’s Law.^ of Enyland, 3rd Edition, Vol. 14, page 305, section 
549, citing Fermanagh and South Tyrone Division Fuse (1956), cited in 
lOo L,Jo.594, although, at one time, a different view' ttjqusars to have pre- 
vailed on the jioiiit, vide Reg rersns Mayor of Tewkesbury (186*8) L.U.3 
(1.B.629. This latter (;ase, how’ever, is regarded as overruled by Lady 
Sandhurst’s case, cited above (vide Roffcrx on Elections Vol. II, page 83 
and Vol. Ill, pages 86 and 87). The ])reponderent view also seems to be 
that it is not in resjiect of every disqualification that the question would 
arise of “thniwn away” votes, even wlu‘re the votes are cast with notice or 
knowledge of the dis(|ualification or of the facts, creating it, but that it 
arises only where the distjualificatiou is founded on some ismitive and definite 
fact, existing oi‘ established at the time of the poll and the passages, (!ite<l 
by Mr. Kar fr(»m llalsbury’s Laws of Enylo nd , have reference to that aspect 
of the matter. Those j)assages, however, state only i)art of the law on the 
]ioiut and it is an incomidete statement of the same without the subsequent 
passagt‘s which run as follows: 

“For the votes, given for a candidate to l>e thrown away the voters 
must, before voting, cither have had or be deemed to have hajl 
notice of the facts, creating the candidate’s disqualihcaiion. It 
was not necessary to show that the elector was aware of the legal 
result that such a fact entailed disqualification. Votes given 
without such notice are good,” 

and which are followed by the very significant passage to the effect that, 
“if, after deducting the votes, given after such notice, from the total 
number of votes, given for the disqualified candidate, he remains in a 
majority, the minority candidate cannot be seated and there must be a fresh 
election”. This passage, last quoted above, unmistakably shows that the law 
is not as contended for by Mr. Kar but that it has been correctly set out by 
us al)ove. In Rogers on Elections also, we find a similar statement of the 
law, so far as the requirement of notice or k«)nwledge is concerned, where 
the learned author says that “votes may be h»st or thrown away by votini;- 
for a candidate, who is disqualified, after notice of disqualification or w'ith 
knowledge of the <lisqualifi<'ation or of the fact, creating it”, vide Vol. IT 
i Eorliomenitirif Elections), page 80 and Vol. ITT (Mnnir.iiml and other 
Elections), page 84, and, in the c«»ursc of discussion, all the relevant ca.s<*s 
on the )>oint including Ijadv Sandhurst’s tsase, cited and relied on bv 
Mr. Kar. are discussed and <*<immented upon and explained by the learned 
author and he then sums up the “knowledge” part of the law as follows: 

“The result of the above decisions is that an elector, who votes for a 
dis(]ualified candidate, with knowledge either of the disqualifica- 
tion or of the facts, creating the disqualification, throws away his 
vote; and such knowledge will be presumed where the disqualifica- 
tion, or the facts, creating the disqualificatitm, are notorious”. 

We do not think that the law is different w'here there is notice in place of 
knowledge and the foregoing discussion will amitly bear that out.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 

TIm* r;ite of maternity benetii payable to the tea garden workers in West 
Ilengal under llie West lieiigal Maternity Benefit (Tea Estates) Aet, 194S 
was fixed on ilie recommendation of a tripartite conference held in 1047 
when the average daily wage of a tea garden worker was much lower. The 
wa^es ol th(j tea garden workers have since been revised. 

The Bill is intended to enhance the rate of maternity benefit payable to 
the tea garden workers commensurate with the increase in wages and is based 
on the agreement between the representatives of employers and employees.

Exhibit A is a riotite of Mi. Acton, the Manager of Fort William Jute 
Mill, dated the Hist August 1940, by which the waste bonus for the Weav- 
ing Tjine Sardars was introduced. This notice clearly shows that the waste 
bonus is in inverse proportion to the quantity of waste collected. Exhibit 
B is a luuster roll for the Weaving Line Sardars t<5r the week ending 
7th Septeinbor 1946. It was shown that weaver Nos. 9. 11 and 20 were 
paid much less than the other weavers by way of waste bonus. From this, 
it was sought to be shown that the maximum rates of 3 annas and 4 annas 
for hessian and sacking looms, respec.tively, were not paid to all in the 
month of September 1946. At the time of the argument of the learned 
spokesman tor the Company, it was brought to my notice that payment on 
a sliding scale was also made on some occasions in the year 1949. although 
tlie hook showing this was not marked us an exhibit in this case. Exhiliii 
1 IS a letter of the Assistant Labour (’’ommissioner, dated the 28th Januarv 
1957, to the Afanager of the Comi»uuy, stating that all the Sardars were 
gi^i'H wii'itc hotitis at the flat rate of .‘I annas and 4 anna.", resjiectively, per 
loi.ni pel u(>ek for hessian and sacking and recommending that this schena' 
of ])ayment should not he disturbed by making payments to them accorci- 
ing to the (iiiality of their work in respect of the waste yarns collected. 
Exhibit 2 is a copy of the letter, dated the 21st Fidnuary 1957, from the 
Manager of the Company addressed to the Assistant Labour Commissioner, 
Hon rah. This letter shows that the Alanager states that the “waste hoiiu'” 
is an incentive given to check the unnecessary wastage of yarns and if this 
“prize’ is withilrawii, there w'ould be no check for wastage, resulting in 
the loK‘ of tile Coiuiiaiiy’s iiroperty. The Alanager also states that “it will 
not he juslified to continue any extra privilege which has been given so 
long to file workers by mistake and the continuance of this extra privilege 
is not justified,” 

Oi« a careful consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case, 
it appears to me that the scheme of payment of waste bonus was introdined 
by the Manager. Mr. Acton, in August 1946 with a view to check the waste 
of yams at the w’eaving looms aud the waste bonus was conceived lo lie 
paid on a sliding scale in the inverse proportion to the quantity of waste 
collected by the Sardars. The evidence on record shows that iiaymeiit on 
the sliding scale on the scheme of Air. Acton, as shown in Exhibit A. was 
made ill Sept'uuher 1946, as shown in Exhibit B. The learned spokesiiuiu 
for the Company also mentioned before me the case of payment on the same 
sliding scale in 1949 os shown in a muster roll of that year, although 
boidi was uot marked as an exhibit, as it w'as produced al the time of th^ 
nrg'umeiits. Accepting that payment at the sliding scale was also made in 
1949, there is no evidence that any payment on such sliding scale of wasl** 
bonus was made in the subsequent years till it w'as revived in 1950, wlieo 
the present disjmfe arose between the Company and the Weaving 
Sardars. The change of Management took place in 1952. Even al 
time of Ihe Management of Messrs. Kettlewell Bullen & Co., Ltd.. 
nients apjiear to have been made at the flat rate of 3 annas for hessian leom' 
and 4 annas for sacking looms from 1960 to 1952. During the time of fh^ 
preseni Management also the same flat rate of payment was made till 
dispute arose in 1956. It may be mentioned that this waste bonus is I'-V' 
able only to the Weaving lane Sardars who were in service aud ’ i 

receipl of this bonus at a date prior to the date of the award of 
.Tuie Textile Tribunal. The evidence of O.P.W. 1 shows that the 
Line Sardars appointed after the date of the Third Omnibus J’ute 
an> being paid at the standard rate mentioned in that award.

In the matter of an industrial dispute existing between The Daily Lolunanya,

BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 

Present: 

Shri M. N. GAN, Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal. 

Appearances: 

For the Workmen: Shri N. D. Manna, Counsel. 

For the Company: Shri P. K. Ghosc. 

This industrial dispute between The Daily Lokinanya (hereinafter referred 
to as the Company) and their working journalists, in respect of the following 
ten issues, was referred to the First Industrial Tribunal by the Government of 
West Bengal, I.abour Department, order No. 431 l-Dis|D|13L-5|55, dated the 
26th September 1956. 

The issues are — 

( 1 ) Whether the termination of services of iSudarna Prosad Singh and 

Girija Prosad Singh was justified? To what relief by way of rein- 
statement and|or compensation are they entitled? 

(2) Introduction of pay scales. 

(3) Hours of work. 

(4) Holidays, 

(5) Leave Rules. 

(6) Introduction of the following amenities: — 

(a) Canteen, (A) Retiring Room, (c) Reference Library and (d) Trans- 
port for night staff, 

(7) Provident Fund, 

(8) Retrenchment Benefits. 

(9) Realisation of arrear pay, 

(10) Bonus. 

Parties filed their written statements before that Tribunal and the case was 
pending for some time for adjudication. By a subsequent order No. 4496-1. R-! 
I.R.| 13L-9|57, dated the 28th November 1957, the Labour Department withdrew 
that case from that Tribunal under section 33B of the Industrial Disputes Act 
and transferred the same to this Tribunal for speedy disposal. Parties did ac)t 
fil6 any separate written statement before this Tribunal and proceeded to tna' 
on the pleadings already filed by them before the First Industrial Tribunaf 
Learned Advocate for the parties have adopted written statements already 
wfore the First Industrial Tribunal as their written statement in this proceeding 
before this Tribunal. After several adjournments for amicable settlement, tn

:ase was fixed for hearing on the 18th July 1958 when the Company filed a 
petition challenging the jurisdiction of this Tribunal to adjudicate on this dispute, 
rhis was heard on the date fixed, along with the whole case, and I decided to 
proceed to adjudicate the case on merits. The reasons tor rejecting the Com- 
pany's objection regarding the jurisdiction of this Tribunal are recorded below; 

The additional issue raised by the Company is whether this Tribunal has 
jurisdiction to entertain and adjudicate the issues under the reference. 
The point formulated by the learned Advocate for the Company is 
this: The original reference in this case was made on the 26th Sep- 
tember 1956 by which the issues in the dispute were referred to First 
Industrial Tribunal. The reference was withdrawn by the Govern- 
ment purporting to act under section 33B, Industrial Disputes Act. 
which came into operation on the 10th March 1957, vide the Calcutia 
Gazette, dated the 4th April 1957, publishing a notification of the 
Ministry of Labour, Government of India, dated the 1st March 1957. 
That section cannot have any retrospective operation so as to apply 
to proceedings started under the old Act, before its amendment, as 
in this case. Therefore, the order of transfer made by the Govern- 
ment of West Bengal under section 33B, Industrial Disputes Act, is 
bad in law and this Tribunal has no jurisdiction to adjudicate and|or 
to proceed with the reference. Learned Counsel on behalf of the 
Union refuted this argument contending that the provisions of section 
33B, Industrial Disputes Act, apply to this case, as it applies to all 
proceedings under this Act and that apart from the provisions of 
section 33B, Industrial Disputes Act, this Government has powers 
under section 21 of the General Clauses Act to transfer, to withdraw 
a reference from one Tribunal and transfer it to another. 

The Industrial Disputes (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 
1956 (No. 36 of 1956), was passed on the 28th August 1956. It 
contained several sections, all of which did not come into force on 
one day. It would appear from the Calcutta Gazette, dated the 4th 
April 1957, mentioned above, that several clau.ses and sections of the 
Act No. 36 of 1956 amending the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, came 
into force on different dates and section 33B, Industrial Disputes Act, 
came into force on the 10th March 1957. Accordingly, on the date 
of transfer on the 28th November 1957 the powers under section 33B 
were there and there cannot be any reasonable objection to the 
exercise of the said powers under that section of the Act. Further, 
it has been conceded that the Government has powers under section 
21 of the General Clauses Act to transfer the reference from one 
Tribunal to another. This has been held by a Division Bench of 
the Calcutta High Court in a case between Bircn Kumar Chatterjee 
and other ver.vwj Reliance Jute Mill Company Limited reported in 
1958 (II) Labour Law Journal, page 67. Further, the wording of 
the section 33B would go to show that the power is conferred on the 
appropriate Government in respect of any proceeding under this Act 
and, therefore, it is idle to contend that the said power can only be 
exercised prospectively to proceedings commencing from the 10th 
March 1957. Any such interpretation is likely to come into open 
conflict with the express provisions of section 33B, Industrial Disputes 
Act. Lastly, there is nothing in the Act to show or .suggest that section 
33B has got no retrospective operation. One of the leading rules 
relating to interpretation of statutes is that every statute, which takes 
away or impairs vested rights acquired under existing law. must be 
presumed to be intended not to have any retrospective operation. But 
this presumption does not apply to enactments affecting procedure or 




501(1 


THE CAE. (JAZ., EXTliV., SEPT. 27. 1058 


Jl- 


Ai:| 


practice as in this case. The reason is that no person has a vcMi 
right in any case of procedure. The general procedure, indeed, .socr 
to be that alterations in the proceedings are always retrospective, unit 
there be some good reasons against it. Learned Advocate for t 
Company could not assign any reason whatsoever why a provisK 
for transfer should not apply to pending cases. For all these reasor 
1 am afraid I cannot accept the Company’s contention as sound. Tl 
result, therefore, is that the transfer of the reference to this Tribun 
is valid and this Tribunal has jurisdiction to entertain undjor to prom 
with this adjudication of this reference. The Company’s petition ( 
objection, therefore, fails.

AWARD 

An industrial dispute between Messrs. Bhartia Electric Steel Co., Ltd. 
(hereinafter referred to as the Company), 8 Swinhoe Street, Calcutta, and their 
workers as represented by Bhartia Iron and Steel Workers’ Union, 7|2A Jamir 
Lane, Calcutta-19, in respect of the following issue was referred to me for 
adjudication by the Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, order 
No. 4615-I.R.|IR|11L-120|57, dated the 3rd December 1957.

Issue 

Whether all the workmen are entitled to get the benefit of the existing 
Incentive Bonus? If so, on what condition? 

Both parties filed written statements, adduced evidence, and advanced 
arguments in the case. 

Issue No. 1: At the outset Shri Khaitan on behalf of the Company contends 
that this reference relates only to the Swinhoe Street Works at Ballygunge and 
it does not apply to the Khardah Works. Shri Khaitan makes a points reference 
to the wording of the order of reference in this case and points out that the 
reference clearly mentioned the Company’s office at 8 Swinhoe Street, Calcutta, 
where there is a factory of the Company and the reference in question was also 
sent to the said address, and not to the address of the Head Office of the Company 
•or to its Khardah Factory. Shri Khaitan further points out that a dispute on 
•certain establishment or more than one establishment can be referred to a 
Tribunal under section 10(5) of the Industrial Disputes Act. A reference has 
been invited to a decision of the Madras High Court in a case between India 
Tyre & Rubber Co. and their workmen reported in 1957 L.L.J. Vol. 11, pages 
5061512, where an interpretation of “industrial establishment” was given by the 
Hon’ble Court. In my view this contention appears to be correct. The present 
reference relates to workers employed at 8 Swinhoe Street, Calcutta only, and 
not at other places. 

The short ppint involved in this case is whether all the workmen are entitled 
to get the benefit of the existing incentive bonus, and if so, on what condition? 

The incentive bonus scheme exists for the benefit of the workiiicn. 
Admittedly, it does not apply to all the workmen employed in the non-productive 
departments. They do not enjoy the benefit of the scheme. The question now 
is whether under the existing scheme all the workmen are entitled to incentive 
bonus. The issue is not for a revision of the existing scheme so as to make it 
applicable to all workmen. Neither is it for preparation of a new scheme for 
those who are not covered by the existing scheme. According to the Union, 
803 workmen including the monthly-rated staff numbering 202, out of the total 
of 3,000, are not covered by the existing scheme. These workmen including the 
temporary hands are employed in the six departments as mentioned in ihc 
paragraph 12 of the Union’s written statement. On the other hand, the 
Company’s case is that only 230 workers, and the piece-rated workers numbering 
288 of the Machine Shop, as stated in Exhibit A(2), do not get the benefit of 
this scheme. As stated above, a number of workmen, particularly, those 
■employed in the non-productive departments are not covered by the scheme. 
The Company’s contention is that for obvious reasons they are not in the scheme, 
and they are not entitled to the benefit of the existing scheme. The Union’s 
contention, however, is that the benefit of the scheme which is confined to 
workmen employed in the productive department should be extended to all, no 
matter where they are employed. The reason is that the production depends 
on the co-operative effort of all sections of the workmen, and every one has a 
share in the total output. So, there should not be any discrimination in the 
matter of granting the benefits of the incentive scheme between workers ami 
workers. The work-load of every individual has increased, and it is only fair 
nnd reasonable that all should derive some benefit out of the scheme in question. 
Further, there are engineering concerns who have similar incentive bonus scheme'^ 
applicable to all workmen. The oral evidence in this case is very short. Shri 
B. N. Majumder, President of the Union, deposed on behalf of the workmen, 
and O.P.W. 1, Shri K. N. Shivaram. deposed on behalf of the Company. Shn 
Ram Sen on behalf of the Union relied on the Exhibit 2, which is a copy of an 
agreement between the Joy Engineering Works and its workmen on production 


Paet I] THE CAL. GAZ., EXTRY., SEPT. 27, 1958 


6023 


bonus, and contended that the workmen employed there get the benefit of the 
scheme no matter where they once employed. Exhibit 2 shows the outline 
of the scheme introduced as a result of an agreement entered into between the 
management and the Workers’ Union on 12th April 1956. The two other awards 
referred to in this connection on behalf of the parties are of Shri G. Palit in the 
case of Messrs. Guest, Keen & Williams Ltd. In one case the learned Judge has 
refused to extend the benefits of the scheme to all and in another, while revising 
the production bonus scheme, made it applicable to all workmen. As stated 
already, this Tribunal is not called upon in this reference to revise the existing 
bonus scheme or to prepare one so that the workmen who are not getting the 
benefits of the scheme at the present time, would get the same. It has been 
conceded that under the existing scheme, numbering about 50, all the workmen 
are not entitled to the benefits of the scheme. Shri Ram Sen pleades that in 
the interest of peace, and in the interest of the success of the scheme itself, its 
benefit should be extended to all the workmen. He advances two more reasons 
for this, viz., (/) to secure co-operation of all concerned so as to get full work 
and («) every one has a share of contribution towards greater production under 
the incentive bonus scheme. This, in his opinion, will ensure industrial peace 
and remove the present discrimination in the matter of payment. The outlines 
of the scheme, the number of which is about 50, arc given in the Exhibit A and 
its work ng in Exhibit A(l). A glance at the scheme will show that, more or 
less, all of them are on experimental basis, and they arc revised from time to 
time. They arc not the conditions of service and their withdrawal does not lead 
to any industrial dispute. They guarantee normal wages. The number of 
workmen concerned in different schemes vary from 4 or 5 to 300 and more. 
No two schemes can be interchanged. Each scheme is tailored according to 
requirement appertaining to operations of that department. The Union's claim 
is that the benefit of the existing scheme should be extended in the same manner 
and on the same terms to everybody. That is to .say the incentive bonus sh»Mild 
he equally distributed so that the present ratio between the quantum of production 
bonus and the wages be maintained. The Union's evidence is that the iemporary 
hands do not get the benefit of this scheme, and the monthly-rated staff also, c.g., 
clerks of the general department, do not get the benefit of the scheme even \^’hen 
thc\ are deputed to work in a productive department where the scheme is in 
operation. I have given my anxious consideration to the evidence and ihc 
circumstances of the case. In my view the production bonus is never looked 
upon as a part of the normal wage, and it is not under the existing scheme. The 
sclieme is not compulsory' in the sense that a workman docs not stand to lose 
even a part of his normal wages, he being not able to qualify liimself for the 
benefit of the scheme. It is not in evidence in this case that the workmen who 
are at present outside the scheme and work outside normal hours, arc not paid 
an\ overtime for overtime work. .The departments in the factory arc, no doubt, 
inter-connected in this sense that one is to some extent dependent on the other. 
It is equally tnie that co-operation of all employees is necessary for the successful 
working out of any scheme. But that alone is not suflicient to iustih a claim 
for a share in the incentive or production bonus even in a non-productive 
department. It may be that in one or two engineering coneems the benefit of 
the incentive scheme has been extended to all workmen. We have already seen 
that in one case this was done on mutual consent of the parties. In another 
case the entire scheme was revised and the issue before the Tribunal was for 
such a revision of the scheme. In another case this was revised. .So there is 
no practice in any engineering concern to extend the benefit of the incentive bonus 
scheme, as a rule, to all workmen. The Union, in my view, has failed to 
establish any reasonable justification for extending the benefits of the scheme to 
workmen who arc now not coyered by any one of them. There is no nroof <m 
the Union's side that there has been any case of discriminatory treatment in the 
matter of application of the scheme or in the matter of payment under the 
scheme. Broadly speaking, the Union’s point of yiew is that all should recciye 



6024 


THE CAL. OAZ., EXTRY., SEPT. 27, 1058 


[Paht I 


equal treatment in this mtUter. It is, no doubt, desirable that equal treatment 
should be meted out to all places in equal circumstances. In that view ci tite 
matter, there has not been any discriminatory treatment in this case. All the 
workmen are not entitled to the benefit of the scheme. 

This is my award. 

M. N. GAN, 

Judge, 

The 30th August 1958. 

By order of the Governor, 

N. R. SIRCAR, 

Asst. Secy, to the Govt, of West Bengal. 


M. N. GAN, 

Judge, Fourth Industrial Tribunal.

Rules

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 

The object of the Bill is to eliuiinate perjury from law courts aud to 
encourag'e ainonpi’Ht the litigant public the habit of speakiug^ the truth. A 
statutory Kuurantee to the acc.used for making a false statement as provided 
for in section 342 of the (Jode of Criminal Procedure, 1898, is repugnant to 
modern notions of jurisprudence and should be deleted. Similarly amongst 
the extenuating* cireumstancen which the (iourt may take into consideration 
at the time of applying provisions of section 562 of the Co(ie of Criminiil 
1 rocedure, 1898, it may also l)e considered if the offender has made a clean 
breast of things concealing nothing. 

intended to achieve the object by amending sections 342 and 
562 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, in the manner indicated 
above.

PART mA Ordinances promulgated by the Gov^ernor of West Bengal under the Constitution of India. 


GOVERNMENT OF WEST BENGAL 


Law Department 
Legislative 

West Bengal Ordinance No. IX of 1958 

THE WEST BENGAL ANTI-PROFITEERING 
ORDINANCE, 1958. 


Whhreas it is expedient in the public interest to prevent 
profiteering in certain articles in daily use; 

And wherlas both Houses of the legislature of West 
Bengal are not in session and the Governor is satisfied that 
circumstances exist which render it necessary for her to lake 
immediate action; 

And whereas the instructions of the President under the 
proviso to clause {1} oi article 213 of the Constitution of India 
have been obtained; 

The Governor is pleased, in exercise of the power conferred 
by clause ( / ) of the said article, to make and promulgate the 
following Ordinance, namely: — 

Short titio 1. (7) This Ordinance may be called the West Bengal 

and extent. Anti-profilccring Ordinance, 1958. 

(2) It extends to the wht)le of West Bengal. 


Dofinitiona. 


2. In this Ordinance, unless there is unytliing repugnant in 
the subject or context. — 


(«) 


(h) 


iO 

(d) 


“dealer" means any person carrying on the business of 
selling any scheduled article, and includes a 
producer, importer, wholesaler or retailer; 
“importer" means any person who brings any scheduled 
article into the State of West Bengal from any 
place outside the State for the purpose of sale in the 
State; 

“producer" means a person engaged in the production, 
manufacture, or prcKCssing of any scheduled 
article; 

“orofitecring”. with its grammatical variations and 
cognate expressions, mean', the sale by a dealer of 
any .scheduled article at a price or rate higher than 
that peiinitted under section 3;

Ihe West Bengal Ami-profiteering Ordinance, 1958 
{Sections 3 — 7.) 

(<*) “retailer” means a person who sells any scheduled 
article to a consumer; 

(/) “scheduled article” means an article specified in the 
First Schedule; and 

{g) “wholesaler” means a person who sells any scheduled 
article to a retailer, and includes a broker, commis- 
sion agent or any other agent having authority to 
sell any scheduled article belonging to his principal. 

3. (7) The State Government may, by order notified in 
the Official Gazette, fix in respect of any scheduled article the 
maximum price or rate which may be charged by a dealer. 

(2) Any order made under sub-section (7) may fix the 
maximum prices or rates for the same description of scheduled 
articles differently in different localities or for different classes 
of dealers, 

4. Any dealer who profiteers in any scheduled article shall 
be punishable with rigorous imprisonment which may extend to 
two years or with fine or with both, and any scheduled article in 
respect of which the offence has been committed or such part 
thereof as to the court may seem fit shall be forfeited to the 
Government. 

5. Any dealer who, without reasonable excuse, — 

refuses to sell any scheduled article, or 

(b) refuses to sell any scheduled article at the price or rate 
fixed in respect thereof under section 3, 

shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment which may 
extend to two years or with fine or with both. 

Explanation , — The possibility or expectation of obtaining a 
higher price for a scheduled article at a later date shall not be 
deemed to be a reasonable excuse for the purposes of this 
section. 


6. (7) Every dealer shall, on requisition by an officer 
duly authorised in this behalf by the State Government by order 
notified in the Official Gazette, submit to him in the form 
specified in the Second Schedule by such date and relating to 
such period as mav be mentioned in the requisition, returns of 
stocks of any scheouled article acquired, held or sold by him. 

(2) Every dealer shall — 

(a) keep in the form specified in the Third Schedule a true 

account of any scheduled article acquired held or 
sold by him after this Ordinance comes into force; 

(b) display in his place of business in a prominent manner 

so as to be ^n to public view, a list of scheduled 
articles intend^ for sale with the prices or rates, if 
any, fixed in respect thereof under section 3; 

(c) furnish to any officer referred to in sub-section (7) or 

any police officer referred to in sub-section (2) of 
section 9 any information in respect of the acquisi- 
tion or sale by him of any scheduled article; 

(d) make available to any officer mentioned in clause (c) 

for his inspection such accounts, registers, 
vouchers or other documents relating to the import, 
production, purchase or sale of any scheduled 
article or matters connected therewith as may be 
required by him. 

7. When any police officer not below the rank of a Sub- 
Inspector of Police has reasonable grounds for believing that 
there has been a contravention of any of the provisions of this 
Ordinance, such officer may, after recording in writing the 
grounds of his belief, at all reasonable hours enter and search 
any place where a dealer keeps, or is for the time being keeping, 
any scheduled article, accounts, registers, vouchers or other 
documents referred to in clause (d) of sub-section (2) of section 
6, and if necessary, inspect, seize or retain all or any of them 
for so long as they m^ be required for any investigation into 
any offence under this Ordinance.

The West Bengal Anti-profiteering Ordinance, 1958 
(Sections 8 — 12 and the First Schedule,) 

8 « Any dealer who fails to comply with any of the provi- 
sions of section 6 or with a requisition issued thereunder or 
obstructs any officer in the exercise of his powers under section 
7 shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment which may 
extend to six months or with fine or with both. 

9 . (1) All offences punishable under this Ordinance shall 
be cognizable. 

(2) Any police officer not below the rank of a Sub- 
Inspector of Police may arrest without warrant any person 
against vyhom a reasonable complaint has been made or credible 
information has been received of his having been concerned in 
any of the offences punishable under this Ordinance. 

10 . No suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding shall lie 
against any public servant for anything which is in good faith 
done or intended to be done under this Ordinance or any order 
made thereunder. 

11. The Stale Government may, with the previous approval 
of the Central Government by order notified in the Oiiirial 
Gazette, add to the First vSchedule any other article ol daily use. 
and thereupon that Schedule shall be deemed to be amended 
accordingly and the article so added shall be deemed to be a 
scheduled article within the meaning of this Ordinance. 

12. If any order controlling the price at which any essential 
commodity within the meaning of the Essential Commodities 
Act, 1955, has been made before the commencement of this 
Ordinance or is made after such commencement and such 
essential commodity is a scheduled article within the meaning 
of this Ordinance and the order so made extends to the State of 
West Bengal or any part thereof, that order shall have effect in 
the State or part thereof, as the case may be, notwithstanding 
anything inconsistent therewith contained in this Ordinance or 
any order made thereunder.

llegarding the objection on the s«‘ore of estoppel raised against the 
Unions, I should say that it d<»e8 not hnuld much water. Of course, under 
a valid contract the parties cannot be permitted to impugn the said con-

Governmnt was nowhere a party. Besides, Government has done it in

there can be no estoppel {\gainst the statute. So the contention on the 
score of estoppel fails. 

There is allogelher a different objection rai.sed by Shri l*hani Ohosli 
regarding (he legal validitj' of the order of corrigendum, dated 7th June 
1957. He challenges it on the ground that Government is not competeid 
t(i make (he corrigendum as it purports to have done. Correction does not 
mean anything more than making a clerical change. But here certain 
parties are in fact eliminated from the scope of adjudication as a result of 
correction embodied in the corrigendum. It i.s also .said that this is not 
an amendment because no improvement has been effected by it. It amounts 
to cancellalion or rather withdrawal, may be partial, of the reference con- 
cerning certain sections of employees originally imjdeuded. This is said to 
be illegal juid in excess of Government’s j)ower. I, of course, agree that 
the word “correction” used in the said corrigendum has not been a hapfiy 
one. The proper wordings .shoubl have been “in modification of the pre- 
vious <»rder”. 1 also admit that as a result of the said change, the TTeail

been excluded from it. But because of that the said corrigendum amounts 
to cancellation or withdrawal of the order of reference, at least partially, 
I am unable to agree. The original order of reference has not been can- 
celled or withdrawn, — neither wholly nor partially. I find no force in the 
argument that an amendment must nece8.sarily result in improvement. 
“Amendment” means a change by way of modification. That may be hy 
addition of parties or even by striking out of |)arties. Under section 21 of 
the General Clauses Act, the authority w'hich is competent to pass an order 
has also the inherent power to amend, vary or rescind the said order. So 
it cannot be said (hat GoA’eniment has no power to amend or modify its 
order after it has made the order of reference. The learned representativp 
of the Union Shri Ghosh has referred to the ease decided by my brother 
Rhri S. C. Sen Gupta betw^een J. S. Cohen & Co. and Santosh Kumar 
Bhuttacharyva (L.L.J., Vol. TI, }»age 205, 195fi), But the facts there are 
distinguishable from the present one. That wuis a case which was originally 
an “individual dispute”. Later on it was sought to be converted into a 
collectiA’^e dispute by an amended order of reference. So the said amend- 
ment w'as held to be not competent to eradicate the inherent lacuna in the 
original order of reference. T have no quarrel with such proposition of law. 
But in the present case the workmen were impleaded generally in the ordci 
of reference. But Government might have .seen the mistake arising from 
it. In the previous two Omnibus Tribunals only the operatives in (Ih* 
factory were impleaded. After the lapse of these ten years GovernmeiiT 
tliought fit (o make another omnibus reference. But in so doing it described

operatives, and not all workmen. Through inadvertence a generi<‘ term
