MINISTRY OF FOOD AND AGRICULTURE 
(Department of Food) 

ORDERS 

New Delhi, the 1st November 1958 

G.S.R. 1050. — In exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of the Essen- 
tial Commodities Act, 1955 (10 of 1955), the Central Government hereby makes 
the following Order, namely: — 

1. Short title, extent and commencement — (1) Ihis Order may be called 
the West Bengal Wheat (Export Control) Order. 1958 

(2) it extends to the whole of the State of West Bengal. 

(3) It shall come into force at once. 

2. Definitions. — In this Order, unless the context otherwise requires, — 

(a) “export” means to take or cause to be taken from any place within 

the State of West Bengal to any place outside the said State; 

(b) “State Government” means the Government of the State of West Bengal; 

(c) “wheat products” includes maida, wholemeal atta, resultant atta, suji 

and rawa, but does not include bran. 

3. Restrictions on the export of wlieat and its products. — No person shall 
export or attempt to export or abet the export of wheal or wheal products except 
under and in accordance with a permit issued by the Stale Government or by 
any officer authorized by the State Government in this behalf: 


r)458b 


mso 


THE CAL. GAZ.. EXTRY., NOVEMBER 8, 1968 


[Past 1A 


Provided that nothing contained hereto shall apply to the export of wheat 
or wheat products — 

(i) not exceeding five seers in weight m the aggregate by a bona fide t^-avellei 

as part of his luggage; 

(ii) on Government account; or 

(iii) under and in accordance with Military Credit Notes. 

4. Effect of the Order.— The provisions of this Order shall be in addition 
to and not in derogation of the provisions of the Calcutta Wheat (Movement 
Control) Order, 1956. 

5. Powers of entry, search, seizure, etc.— -(1) Any Police Officer not below 
the rank of Assistant Sub-Inspector and any other person authorized in this 
behalf by the State Government may, with a view to securing compliance witf 
this Order or to satisfying himself that this Order has been complied with, — 

(i) stop and search, or authorize any person to stop and search, any person 

boat, motor or any vehicle or receptacle used or intended to be usee 
for the export of wheat or wheat products; 

(ii) enter and search and authorize any person to enter and search an} 

place; 

(iii) seize or authorize the seizure of any article in respect of which he 

suspects that any provision of tliis Order has been, is being or ij 
about to be contravened, along with the packages, coverings oi 
receptacles in which such article is found or the animals, vehicles, 
vessels, boats or other conveyances used in carrying such article 
and thereafter take or authorize the taking of all measures neccssarj 
for securing the production of the packages, coverings, receptacles 
animals, vehicles, vessels, boats or other conveyances so seized, ir 
a court and for their safe custody pending such production. 

(2) The provisions of sections 102 and 103 of the Code of Criminal Proce- 
dure, 1898 (5 of 1898), relating to search and seizure shall, so far as may be, 

apply to searches and seizures under this clause. 204(79)158-PY.II.l 


GSR 1051 In exercise of the powers conferred by section 3 of the Essen- 

tial Commodities Act, 1955 (10 of 1955), the Central Government hereby makes 
the following Order, namely:— 

1 Short title, extent and commencement. — (1) This Order may be callcc 
the Imported Foodgrains (Prohibition of Unauthorized Sale) Order, 1958. 

(2) It extends to the whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir, 

(3) It shall come into force at once. 


2. Definitions.— In this Order, unless the context otherwise requires,— 

(a) “authorized dealer” means a dealer authorized by the Central Govern 
^ ^ ment or a State Government or by a duly authorized ofliccr ol tht 
Central Government or the State Government, to run a fair pna 
shon or ration shop at which imported foodgrains are or miiv be 


(b) “imported foodgrains” means foodgrains imported from outside India 
bv the Central Government and supplied by that Government, citbei 
directly or through a State Government, to authorized dealers )oi 

sale to the public; 

fcl “State” includes a Union territory and “State Government in the cave 
of a Union territory means the Administrator of the Union territory.

PiXOF lA] THE CAL. OAZ., EETBY., NOVEMBER 8, 1968 

3. Frohibilioii of unauthorised sale of imported foodgndna. No person 

other than an authorised dealer shall sell, or store or offer for sale, imported 
foodgrains in any quantity, either split or unsplit or mixed with other grains. 

4. Saving. — ^Nothing in this Order shall apply to — 

(i) the sale or storage for sale of imported foodgrains on Government 

account; or 

(ii) the re-sale by a person of imported foodgrains sold by the Central 

Government or a State Government by auction or by tender; or 

(iii) the sale by a wholesale dealer authorized by the Central Government 

or a State Government to an authorized dealer. 

5. Powers of entry, search, seizure, etc, — (1) Any person authorized by the 
State Government or die Central Government in this behalf may, with a view 
to securing compliant with this Order or to satisfying himself that this Order 
has been complied with, — 

(i) stop and search or authorize any person to slop and search, any person, 

boat, motor or any vehicle or receptacle used or intended to be 
used for movement of imported foodgrains for sale or storage for 
sale; 

(ii) enter and search and authorize any person lo enter and search any place; 

(iii) seize or authorize the seizure of any imported loodgrajns in respect of 

which he suspects that any provision ol this Order has been, is being 
or is about to be contravened along with the packages, coverings or 
receptacles in which the imported foodgrains are found or the 
animals, vehicles, vessels or conveytmees used in carrying the 
imported foodgrains and thereafter take or authorize the taking of 
all measures necessary for securing the production of the packages, 
coverings, receptacles, animals, vehicles, vessels or conveyances so 
seized in a court and for their safe custody pending such production. 

(2) The provisions of sections 102 and 103 of the Code of Criminal Proce- 
dure, 1898, relating to search and seizure shall, so far as may be, apply to 
searches and seizures under this clause.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 

Section 20 of the Calciitta Tliika Tenancy Act, 1949 (West Bengal Act 
11 of 1949) requires tliat the rent tlejmsited with the Controller hv a thika 
tenant under section 17 should be forwarded to the landlord by the Con- 
troller by postal money order. This is eausin^r ditticulty as the landlords 
are refusinK to ae.cejd the money so forwarded. 

Difficulty has also arisen with regard to 8U]>|dy of electricity to a thika 
tenant. Supitly ol electricity to such a tenant recjuires previous consent 
of the owner of the land which is often refused. 

The Bill has boen framed 'with the object of removiim fhi* above 
difficulties.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 


The Standards of Weights and Measures Act, 1950 (89 of 19r)(i), which 
seeks to establish standards of weights and measures based on the metric 
system lor the entire country, has been brought into force by the Govern- 
ment of India to a limited extent simultaneously all over India with effect 
ironi Ist October, 1958. 

2. Eurther, in the absence of any Standards of Widghts and Measures 
Act, and an Enforcement OrganLsation therefor in this State, there remains 
the constant risk of deception in all transactions for trade or commerce, 
especial iy of the credulous and silent classes of consumers. Barring a few^ 
sectiojis of the Jiidian Penal Code this State Government have no weapon 
lo com hat dishonest traders and lu’otect the consuming public, from their 
cliitidjes 


3- As the enforcement of standards of weights and measures is a State 
responsibility under Entry No. 29 of the State List, this State Government 
is reijuired to enact a complementary legislation for enforcement of weights 
and measures based on the metric system. 

d. As it was necessary to take c.ertain preliminary steps in advance of 
the Central Gov(*rnment’s notified date of onforcement of metric system of 
weights and measures, i.e., 1st October, 1958, and as the Tjegislature was not 
in session, the West Bengal Standards of Weights and Measures (Enforce- 
ment) Ordinance, 1958 (West Ben. Ord. No. VII of 1958) was promulgated 
hy the Governor on 24th September, 1958. The Bill is intended to replace 
the Ordinance by an Act of the State Legislature.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


In the recent past, there was a sudden and sharp rise in the prices of 
certain essential commodities and the indications were that there might be 
iurther increase in prices. As the State Government was of the view that 
there w^is little or no justification for such rise in prices, it was considered 
necessary to adopt measures for checking tlie rise in prices and preventing 
profiteering by dealers in such essential commodities. It was with this 
object that the West Bengal Anti-profiteering Ordinance, 1958 (West Ben. 
(h’d. rX of 1958) w'as promulgated by the Governor of West .Bengal on 
tlie 2:ind October, 1958 when tlie Legislature waxs not in session. 

Tlie present Bill, which will replace the said Ordinance, contains provi- 
sions empowering Government to fix the maximum prices of certain 
essential commodities mentioned in the Schedule to the Bill and to take 
action to check profiteering in such commodities. ,

8TATEM€NT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 

The Law Kevision Committee (now State Law Commission) pointed out 
certain defects^ and omissions in the Calcutta Official Receiver’s Acd, 19d8 
^Bengal Act VJl of 19d8). The existing provisions in the A<*t regarding 
receipt, withdrawal, payment and investment of moneys by the Official 
Receiver are not in conformity with the provisions of the C-onstitution of 
Jndia. Under Arti(de 284(/i) of the Constitution the moneys received by or 
deposited with the Official Receiver are required to be paid into the public, 
account of the State. As, however, investment of monevs out of the public 
account will not be permissible until any law or rule is made in that 
res])ecl under Article 28d(:^) of the Constitution, the Offictial Re(*eiver is 
required to be authorised to withdraw sums deposited in the public account, 
as and when necessary, for the purpose of making various prescribed pay- 
ments and investments. It is necessary to remove the defects and omissions 
and to provide for certain other matters by amending the Act. The Bill 
has been drawn up for that purpose.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 



Since tlie umlertakinf? of tiie Steel Projec t at Durgapur in the district of 
Burdwan^ structures have been and are being erected in an unplanned 
manner in and around the area. Large-scale speculation of land is also 
going on there, Goyeriiment are undertaking vai'ious other schemes such as 
Coke Oven, Gas Grid, etc. in the vicinity of the area. It is, therefore, 
necessary to obtain powers for the State (ioverninent to prevent unplanned 
constructions and speculation in lands in the area. 

The Bill has been framed with the above objects in view. The main 
features of the Bill are as follows : — 

(1) Constitution of the Durgajiur Development Authority with powers 
to control unplanned constructions and to give directions fur 
their stoppage, alteration or even demolition. 

(i) Acquisition of the land in the case of the inability of any person to 
comply with the directions of the Durgapur Development 
Authority, on the application of the said person. 

(3) Empowering tho Durgapur Development Authority or any other 

person or officer to lay down, place, maintain, alter, remove or 
repair any pipes, pipe-lines* supply-lines, posts, or other 
appliances or apparatus for the maintenance of supplies and 
services essential to the life of the community. 

(4) Imposition of penalty for violation of the directions given by the 

Durgapur Development Authority.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 

The amendments proposed in the Bill are intended to remove certain 
anomalies and i)ractical difficulties experienced in working the Act and to 
clarify ('crtain i)rovisions of the Act. 

The Act was originally i)a8sed in 1956 but was ultimately published as 
Act 1 of 1957. So, the Act is now proposed to be called the West Bengal 
Panchayat Act, 1957 [clause 2 and clause 14(a) of the .Bill]. 

According to the scheme of the Act, the Anchal Panchayat is the 
j)rincipal local authority. It is, therefore, sought to make the election of 
the Pradhan of an Anchal Panchayat the starting point of affecting the 
operation of other Acts enumerated in Schedule 1 to the Act [clause 3(a)]. 

The Bihar Panchayat Itaj Act is in force in the territories transferred 
from Bihar to West Bengal. Provision is made for its repeal [clause 14(5)], 
and consequential amendments are proposed [clause 3(5)]. 

To guard against eventualities, provisions are made for appointment of 
the members of a (iraw Panchayat by the State Government on the failure 
of the (rrani Sahha to elect such members and for prescribing the time and 
manner of their ele<'tion (clause 4 and clause 13), and also for the trans- 
action of the normal business of a (rram Pa<richayat during the period 
between the expiry of the term of ajipointed members and the commence- 
ment of tlie (erm of elected members (clause 5). 

Similar proxisions arc reejuired for appointment of the members of an 
Anrha! Pani'haynt. U is also necessary to eliminate the conflict between 
liie tour-year term ot office of the members of an Anchal Panchayat and the 
one-year Itoiii of office of the memht'rs of a Gram Panchayat appointed 
under scM tion 13. According to the present rule 9 of the West Bengal 
Panchayat Buies, 1958 a notice of at least sixty days has to be given before 
an election; tlie time for filling up a vacancy in an Anchal Panchayat has, 
therefore, to be extended from two to tliree months. A person may be 
allowed to be a member both of a Gram Panchayat and an Anchal 
Panchayat, Provisions are made accordingly (clause 6). 

But a i)crson should be debaired from holding the office both of 
Adh yaksha ar ( padhyahsha of a Gram Panchayat and a Pradhan or 
Pfudhan of an Anchal Pancimyat (clause 7). ^^rovisions are also necessary 
to be made for mdifyiug the election or ap])ointment of the members of an 
Ancliul PancJuiyaf and of its Pradhan and G pa-P radhan (clause 8). 

A A yaya Panchayat is to consist of five members elected from amongst 
the members of Gram Sahhas wdthin an Anchal Panchayat; where an 
An dull Panchayat comprises more than five Gram Sahhas it is necessary 
to provide that at the time of election no Grain Sahha may be left out of 
(onsideration. So, the second proviso to section 70(2) of the Act is 
u • * L 9)* In a suit, the accrual of the cause of action 

wutlun the local limits of a Nyaya Panchayat should be sufficient to give it 
.lurisdietion apart from the residence of tne defendant, and section 83 of 
the Act IS amended accordingly {clause 10). It is expressly provided that 
he members of a Nyaya Pcmch^yat are public servants (clause 11).

As the repeal of certain enuctmeuts according to section 4 of the Act 
precedes the constitution oi a Nyaya Panchayat under section 70(7) of the 
Act, it is necessa^ to provide for the transfer of suits and cases pending 
in courts functioning under some of those enactments to the ordinary courts, 
and this is done by substitution of section 118 which in its present form 
is considered unnecessary (clause 12).

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 

It is necessary to amend the West Bpnfi:al Estates Acquisition Act, 1963 
for removing? certain working dilliculties and securing better social justice. 
The Bill seeks to provide tor the following, namely : — 

(1) Acquisition of land comprised in embankment in cases where the 

State Government considers that the maintenance of such 
embankment should be taken over by the State Government in 
the public interest; 

(2) Non“i»aynicnt of compensation to the intermediaries in respect of 

their retained lands and, in lieu tliereof, no collection of rent 
from them for five years from the date of vesting; 

(3) Recovery of sui)erior landlords' dues from subcA’dinate tenure- 

holders according to the share of ea(di c.o-sharer and adjustment 
of such dues against c.omjmnsation payable to them; 

(4) Payment of ad interim. com|>ensation to the internuHliaries in such 

(iases as th(‘ State Gov(*rnment may think fit, even where agree- 
ment has been made under sections 7 and 9 of the Act, and 
paymeni of interesi 1o the limited ownens ; 

(5) Simplification of the procedure for preparation of the (Jompensa- 

tion Assessment Roll; 

(6) Payment of annuity for 20 years to prodinie-paying tenants having 

income up to a certain amount; 

(7) Payment of annuity to any person or institution in rec'eipt of any 

sum charg(‘d against tin*, income of the intermediary from liis 
estates or interests for a religious or charitable purpose; 

(8) Pixatioii of rent at Rs. 9 ^ler iicre for rai/jafs who used to pay rent 

in kind ; 

(9) Other necessary and incideniul matters.

On 

THE WEST BENGAL CHILDREN BILL, 1958

which the West Bengal Children Bill. 11)58, was refened have 
considered the Bill and we have the honour to submit our llepoi't 
to which the Bill as amended by us is annexed. 

1 The Joint Select Committee held five sittings and considered 
the Bill carefully clause by clause. The Committee was asked to 
submit its Report by the 31st August, 1958; but the (.ommittee 
could not do so as it could not finish its deliberations by that date. 
The Committee crave leave of the House to submit its Report now.

4. Having regard to this limited scope of the Bill, the Com- 
mittee found itself unable to take into consideration many of the 
suggestions of the above-mentioned organisations for the general 
welfare of children, e.g., care of children of poor widows or 
crippled and old father, compulsory free primary education, 
providing playgrounds for children, prevention of misery to 
children, banning of unsuitable books and cinema shows, etc., or 
to incorporate them in the Bill. 

5. The Bill is a consolidating Bill; at present the subject 
matter of the Bill is governed by four Acts, viz., the Reformatory 
School Act, 1897, the Bengal Children Act, 1922, the Bengal 
Boi'stal Schools Act, 1928, and partly by the Bengal Vagrancy 
Act. 1943. The Bill has consolidated the provisions of the fore- 
going Acts and amended and modified the law in the light of the 
experience derived during the past and of the requirements of 
modern times. 

6. The main changes which the Joint Select Committee have 
introduced in the Bill are the following: — 

(a) Tt has been provided that Reformatory Schools should be 

of two different classes — one for the reception of 
juvenile delinquents and the other for the reception of 
children other than delinquents; 

(b) The State Government shall appoint a Board of Visitors 

to visit Reformatory, Boi’stal or Industrial Schools and 
to record their comments as regards the management 
of such Schools; 

{(.•) 'I'here shall be a Board called the State Children’s Board 
to advise the State Government regarding all matters 
in relation to the administration of the Act; 

(d) Every child shall, as soon <as he or she is received in a 

School, be examined by a Medical Officer; 

(e) The Government will be empowered to establish or 

recognise after-care organisations for the welfare of 
.juvenile delinquents and other children discharged from 
Reformatory, Borstal or Industrial Schools; 

(f) The Government will also have power to appoint Probation 

Officers to visit juvenile delinquents or other children 
who are taken charge of by after-care associations or 
by parents or other guardians in order to see to their 
proper rehabilitation; 

(g) When a woman with children is sent to prison, the court 

may allow any child not more than two years of age to 
accompany her and m.ay direct any child over two years 
of age to be sent to a reception home or Reformatory 
School of the second type. 

7. Other changes which are of a minor nature or which have 
been made for clarification of meaning, and necessary verbal and 
consequential changes have been shown in their proper places. 

8. Several suggestions were made but the Committee have not 
mund it possible or desirable to incorporate these rigidly in the 
Bill itself. 


It was suggested that a larger proportion of women should be 
employed as Inspectors or Magistrates for the trial of juvenile 
delinquents. Sufficient number of qualified women may not be 
available at present for the purpose. It should, however, be the 
endeavour of the Government to enlist the services of women as 
tar as possible.

MEMORANDUM 

From Shrimati Sudha Mazumdar for consideration of the Joint Committee 
on the West Bengal Children Billi 1958. 

Tho system of with delinquent children in the Netherlands for 

i^iany years has been found to he very satisfa(;tory. It is as follows : — 

A woman social welfare ofKcer-m/w -policewoman is placed in charge of 
a certain zone of the town. It is her duly to watch the area under her 
charge very carefully. When she sees any ( hild being neglected, that is, 
if the child is seen playing about in the sireeis nncared for or ill-treated 
in any manner, she traces the parents or guardian and if it is found that 
the child is neglected on account of step-parents or drunken parents or 
sheer careless parents, they are warned and if this continues in spite of 
the warning then tlie child and its parents are summoned before the 
children’s judge who gives a further warning. If in spite of this the 
child continues to be neglected or ill-treated then it is taken to what is 
cjilJed a Half Freeflow Howe, This Home is in (*harge of a matron and is 
kind of hostel from where th(» child goes to scdiool or continu(vs any 
vocational training that he or she may be undergoing. According to the 
income of the parents they have to ]>ay a certain sum of money for the 
upkeep of the child and the rest is paid by the State. The child can 
stay liere for two years, visit its [)arents or tlu‘ parents can come and see 
tiu child once on a Sunday. There are many Homes like this for boys and 
olluu’s for girls of different ages. There is a cojnmittee to plan the evenings 
when music and gaimvs are organised. The matron is the ‘‘Mother” of the 
children and looks after them very carefully. Ex(*(*pt for having to return 
at this time at a fixed time there is no other restriction that is why it is 
called Half Freedom. Home, 


We can have a few Homes of this kind with (tertain modificationB of 
course but the basic principles may remain the same.

Inspection of Schools! In Reformatories, Borstal school and Industrial

3. In this Act, unless there is anything repugnant in the 
subject or context, — 

(1) “hut” means any structure, no substantial part of which, 

excluding the walls up to a height of eighteen inches 
above the floor or floor-level, is oonstrucUd of masonry, 
reinforced concrete, ferro- concrete, cemented brick- 
work, steel, iron or other metal, or any combination of 
these materials ; 

(2) “notification” means a notification published in the 

Official Gazette ; 

(3) “prescribed” means prescribed by rules made under this 

Act ; 

(4) “prescribed authority” means any person appointed 

by the State Government, by notification, to perform 
all or any of the functions of the prescribed authority 
under this Act ; 

(5) “slum” means any land containing a collection of huts 

or other structures used or intended to be used for human 
habitation ; 

(0) “slum-area” means any area declared as such by the Htate 
Government under section 4. 

4. (1) If the State Government is satisfied that in any area — 

(a) the huts or other structures used or intended to be used for 

human habitation are unfit for such purposes, or 

(b) the unhealthy or unhygienic condition thereof or of the 

huts or other structures therein, is dangerous or 
injurious to public health or to the health of the inhabi- 
tants of the area, 

the fcltate Government may, by notification, and in such other 
manner as may be prescribed, proclaim its inUuition to declare 
such area to be a slum-area, 

(2) Upon the publication of such a notification and within 
Uvo months of such publication, the person or persons affected by 
such notification may make representations in writing to the State 
Government, stating the grounds of their objection to the in- 
tended declaration. 

(3) Upon consideration of such representations, if any, the 
State Govoniment may withdraw the notification mentioned in 
sub-section (1) or may, by notification, declare such area or any 
portion thereof to be a slum-area. 

6. (J) The State Government may, within one year after 
an area has bt^en declared a slum-area under sub-section 

of section 4, acquire the land comprised in such area to- 
getlier with all huts and other structures standing thereon by 
publisliing in the Official Gazette and in such other manner as may 
be prescribed a notice to the effect that the State Govemnient luU 
decided to acquire such land together with all huts and other 
structures standing thereon.
